summary: This note is a clipped Verywell Mind article by Kendra Cherry explaining Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development, which proposes four stages: sensorimotor (birth to 2), preoperational (2 to 7), concrete operational (7 to 11), and formal operational (12 and up). It describes each stage's characteristics, Piaget's view of children as active learners who think differently from adults rather than less intelligently, and key concepts including schemas, assimilation, accommodation, and equilibration. Boilerplate navigation, related-article lists and footer text were ignored.
one_line: Overview of Jean Piaget's four stages of cognitive development and their core concepts such as schemas, assimilation, and accommodation.
key_facts: Jean Piaget's theory suggests children move through four stages of cognitive development.
Piaget's sensorimotor stage runs from birth to 2 years.
Piaget's preoperational stage covers ages 2 to 7.
Piaget's concrete operational stage covers ages 7 to 11.
Piaget's formal operational stage covers age 12 and up.
Piaget early on worked as an assistant to Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon as they standardized their IQ test.
Albert Einstein called Piaget's discovery "so simple only a genius could have thought of it."
Piaget felt development is largely fueled from within, while Lev Vygotsky placed greater emphasis on external factors such as culture.
Piaget's view was that children are not less intelligent than adults; they simply think differently.
In the sensorimotor stage, object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen.
In the concrete operational stage, children begin to understand conservation, such as that a short, wide cup and a tall, skinny glass can hold the same amount of liquid.
The formal operational stage is marked by abstract thinking, deductive reasoning, and reasoning about hypothetical problems.
Assimilation is taking new information into existing schemas, while accommodation is changing existing schemas in light of new information.
Equilibration is the mechanism Piaget said children use to balance assimilation and accommodation, helping them move from one stage to the next.
Piaget wrote that knowing an object means acting upon it, constructing systems of transformations that can be carried out on or with the object.
